subsystems.name: Radio node
subsystems.role: a small computer with one or more radios that both serves local users and relays other nodes' traffic.

subsystems.name: Mesh routing layer
subsystems.role: finds a path for every packet across whichever nodes happen to be up, and reroutes when one fails.
parts: link-state or distance-vector routing protocol (e.g. Babel, OLSR)

subsystems.name: Spectrum plan
subsystems.role: shares scarce unlicensed airtime so nodes do not drown each other in interference.

subsystems.name: Backhaul gateway
subsystems.role: connects the mesh to the wider internet — the part mesh networking cannot replace.

subsystems.name: Power
subsystems.role: keeps rooftop and hillside nodes alive.
parts: solar panel and battery for off-grid sites

subsystems.name: Trust and identity
subsystems.role: keeps an open, volunteer-run network from being trivially abused.

buildSteps.title: Pick the radio bands
buildSteps.detail: High-band Wi-Fi gives hundreds of megabits over line-of-sight links of a few to tens of kilometres; sub-GHz radios like LoRa trade that down to a few kilobits per second for ranges of many kilometres through buildings and trees.

buildSteps.title: Build the node
buildSteps.detail: A processor board, radio cards, antenna connectors and surge protection go into a sealed box that can sit on a mast for years.

buildSteps.title: Site the nodes
buildSteps.detail: Installers mount nodes on rooftops, towers and hills with clear lines of sight, aiming directional antennas at their nearest neighbours.

buildSteps.title: Form the mesh
buildSteps.detail: Each node broadcasts its presence; the routing protocol builds a map of the network and picks paths automatically, with no central server to configure.

buildSteps.title: Add backhaul
buildSteps.detail: A few well-placed nodes are given a wired or licensed-wireless uplink, acting as gateways between the mesh and the global internet.

buildSteps.title: Secure and meter it
buildSteps.detail: Traffic is encrypted node-to-node, and gateways apply fair-use rules so one user cannot consume the whole shared link.

buildSteps.title: Operate and grow
buildSteps.detail: Volunteers or a cooperative monitor links, replace failed hardware, and extend coverage — the network heals around outages because routing simply recomputes.

prerequisites.why: unlicensed Wi-Fi chipsets and low-power wide-area radios are mass-produced and inexpensive.
routing works well for tens to a few hundred nodes but generates heavy overhead as networks grow.
they turn short-range radios into multi-kilometre point-to-point links.

prerequisites.tech: Long-haul capacity that is not carrier-owned
prerequisites.why: data still has to cross continents by submarine fibre or satellite, both owned by large operators — a mesh of local hops cannot span an ocean.
solar and battery systems let nodes run where no mains supply reaches.

pathway.milestone: city and rural community networks in which residents own the routers and share an uplink
pathway.unlocks: low-cost access in places commercial operators skip.

pathway.milestone: disaster and emergency meshes that keep working when cell towers fail
pathway.unlocks: resilient communications for responders and affected communities.

pathway.milestone: device-to-device relays built into phones and vehicles as a standard feature
pathway.unlocks: coverage that thickens automatically wherever people gather.

pathway.milestone: federated regional networks linked by shared, openly governed backbone capacity
pathway.unlocks: meaningful independence from a single ISP, though the global core would still be shared infrastructure rather than a pure peer-to-peer mesh.
